findings.paper_title: AG187 Apdx 1 WCC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit delivery significantly behind target timescales: only 38% of audits issued within agreed deadline for draft reports (target 80%)
findings.detail: KPI data shows only 38% of audits delivered to draft report stage within agreed timescales (target 80%); only 33% delivered to final report within target (target 80%). External quality assessor noted stakeholders commented on occasional delays in audit completion. Audit team identified bottleneck analysis as ongoing action, suggesting resource or process constraints. This delays identification and remediation of governance weaknesses.
findings.matters: Delayed audit completion extends exposure window for identified control weaknesses; indicates possible under-resourcing of audit function or process inefficiency; suggests governance monitoring and control improvement cycles are slower than they should be.
findings.figures: 38% actual vs 80% target (draft reports); 33% actual vs 80% target (final reports)
findings.quote: Audits delivered within agreed timescales (% year to date) o To issue of draft report Ongoing 80% 38% X o To issue of final report Ongoing 80% 33% X

findings.paper_title: AG187 Apdx 1 WCC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: No governance framework for agency staff and consultants; inconsistent compliance with IR35 rules and Agency Workers Regulations requirements
findings.detail: Audit found no formal policy, framework or guidance for engaging agency staff or consultants. IR35 guidance outdated and not reflecting latest legislative changes; inconsistent IR35 assessments with no retained evidence (some managers claim to use HMRC CEST tool but records not retained, others rely on agency confirmation or believe IR35 not required). Agency workers' statutory Day 1 rights and 12-week equal treatment rights not being actively tracked despite being mandatory. Sample testing: only 2 of 6 agency/contractors enrolled on ASPIRE and completed mandatory training. No contracts or service agreements obtained for testing sample. Agency performance managed informally with no formal documentation. Several corrective actions passed agreed implementation dates.
findings.matters: Lack of framework creates compliance risk around employment law, tax status, and procurement rules; undermines council control over contractor spend and reduces transparency; exposes council to regulatory risk (HMRC, Employment Rights).
findings.figures: 2 of 6 contractors enrolled and completed mandatory training; multiple corrective actions past implementation date
findings.quote: There was no framework/policy or guidance in place for use of agency/consultants to ensure roles and responsibilities are clearly defined, consistently applied and aligned with statutory and Council requirements, resulting in notable inconsistencies in the processes followed across departments

findings.paper_title: AG187 Apdx 1 WCC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Building Control failed to submit mandatory annual returns to Building Safety Regulator for 2024 and 2025; mandatory annual management review missed
findings.detail: Building Control required to submit annual QMS return to Building Safety Regulator (BSR) under Operational Standards Rules. No return submitted for 2024; at time of audit, 2025 return also not submitted. Annual management review including KPI reporting was missed in 2024, preventing self-verification of QMS continuing suitability. No documented ongoing controls for performance data analysis as required by LABC QMS Quality Manual. No mechanism in place for gathering customer feedback.
findings.matters: Non-submission represents regulatory non-compliance and puts council's accreditation status at risk; missed management review breaks internal control cycle for service monitoring; indicates governance gap over statutory compliance.
findings.figures: Annual returns: not submitted for 2024 or 2025
findings.quote: A return was not submitted for 2024 and at the time of the audit, had not been submitted for 2025. As the annual management review, including reporting against KPIs, was missed in 2024, Building Control had not self-verified the continuing suitability and effectiveness of the QMS

findings.paper_title: AG187 Apdx 1 WCC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Six unmitigated cyber security risks from Thrive assessment remained incomplete at audit; remediation timescales delayed up to 11 months
findings.detail: Of 30 cyber security risks identified in Thrive assessment, 14 marked complete by audit but only 13 substantiated with evidence; 6 items remained incomplete at time of audit; audit team rated this as 'inadequate for cyber security risks mitigations'; some items took 11 months to complete after Thrive report issued; three dismissed risk items lacked supporting evidence for dismissal and were not reported to senior management.
findings.matters: Unmitigated cyber security risks threaten council data, systems and service continuity; slow remediation of identified risks indicates governance weakness in IT risk management; 11-month timescales for standard remediation suggest inadequate prioritization or resourcing of critical controls.
findings.figures: 30 Risk Identified items; 14 marked complete; 6 incomplete at audit; up to 11 months for completion
findings.quote: Six items remained incomplete at the time of audit, which, in our opinion is inadequate for cyber security risks mitigations. Dismissed Risk Identified items were not reported to the senior management team and evidence to support the reason for the dismissal of three items was not provided.

findings.headline: Audit completion dependent on sustained management cooperation and quality of evidence provision — auditors signaling capacity risk
findings.detail: The auditors explicitly state multiple times that 'Our ability to complete the audit is dependent on the timely formulation of appropriately supported accounting judgements, provision of accurate and relevant supporting evidence, access to the finance team and management's responsiveness to issues identified during the audit.' They note that if the council cannot meet these requirements, the audit timeline will extend further. The council's 2024/25 assessment rated 'Timeliness and quality of evidence supporting key accounting estimates' as 'Requires Improvement.'
findings.matters: The auditors are flagging concerns about the council's finance function capacity and quality of evidence. This suggests the council may struggle to support a timely audit and raises questions about the strength of the finance team.
findings.figures: Audit Results Report deadline 30 November 2026; Auditor's Annual Report by 30 November 2026
findings.quote: Our ability to complete the audit is dependent on the timely formulation of appropriately supported accounting judgements, provision of accurate and relevant supporting evidence, access to the finance team and management's responsiveness to issues identified during the audit. Failure to achieve this will significantly increase the level of resources required to fulfil our respective responsibilities.

findings.headline: Opening reserves balances require detailed risk assessment and historic rebuild — material gaps in evidence for pre-2023/24 balances
findings.detail: The auditors will undertake a detailed risk assessment to evaluate the risk of material misstatement in opening reserves balances at 1 April 2025. They note it is 'likely' they will need to audit transactions and movements for 2022/23 and 2023/24 (and possibly earlier) to rebuild assurance over the historic position. This suggests material gaps in evidence exist for historical balances and that management may lack high-quality working papers for prior years.
findings.matters: The need for a historic rebuild of assurance indicates the council's accounting records or reserves documentation for multiple years may be incomplete or unreliable. This prolongs audit resolution and signals potential historical accounting issues.
findings.figures: Risk assessment to be completed by 30 June 2026; work anticipated on 2022/23, 2023/24 and earlier years
findings.quote: It is likely that we will need to audit certain transactions and movements for 2022/23 and 2023/24 (and earlier years, where applicable) to rebuild assurance over the historic position. Should we proceed with this phase of work, we will require assurances from management that high quality working papers and supporting evidence can be provided

findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in Housing Revenue Account governance and property compliance management remain from prior year
findings.detail: The auditors have identified continued significant weaknesses in property compliance management for HRA properties and governance/internal control within the Housing Service and Property Services Department. This issue spans both governance and value-for-money assessments and was identified in 2024/25 but remains unresolved. The auditors will focus on assessing progress made in delivering the requirements of an action plan by year-end 2025/26.
findings.matters: Unresolved governance weaknesses in a material service area (housing) suggest management has not fully remediated control failures. For lenders, this indicates ongoing operational and compliance risk.
findings.figures: HRA housing stock; weaknesses identified in both 2024/25 and continuing into 2025/26 audit plan
findings.quote: Weaknesses in property compliance management for Housing Revenue Account properties owned or managed by the Council, and governance and internal control within the Council's Housing Service and Property Services Department

findings.headline: £136 million in property assets remain unaudited — prior-year recommendation on PPE/investment property valuations not addressed
findings.detail: Property, Plant & Equipment and Investment Property valued at EUV/FV totalled £67.5 million and £68.7 million respectively in 2024/25. The auditors identified weaknesses in the quality of evidence and assumptions from the external valuer. This was a prior-year issue and the auditors explicitly note the council has not addressed the recommendation. The auditors state it is 'essential that the prior-year recommendation relating to PPE and investment property valuations...is addressed by management to enable us to fully complete our audit procedures in this area.'
findings.matters: Material balance sheet items representing nearly 10% of total assets remain disputed. Inability to audit these assets directly prevents auditors from signing off the financial statements and indicates potential accounting control weaknesses.
findings.figures: PPE valued at EUV/FV: £67.5m; Investment Property valued at EUV/FV: £68.7m (2024/25 audited figures); materiality threshold £2.1m
findings.quote: In the prior year we noted potential errors in the key inputs and disagreed with some of the assumptions used in the valuation of land and buildings valued using EUV and FV. This includes PPE Other Land and Buildings valued at EUV; Surplus Assets valued at FV; and Investment Properties valued at FV.

findings.headline: Disclaimer audit opinion issued in 2024/25 — auditors could not complete their work or express confidence in the financial statements
findings.detail: The Council received a disclaimer opinion in the year ended 31 March 2025, which is the most severe audit outcome available. This means EY could not obtain sufficient evidence to support an audit opinion. The auditors are now in a multi-year recovery programme to rebuild assurance from a disclaimed opinion to an unqualified opinion. The council is 'in line with expected timescales' but this remains a serious indicator of accounting or evidence quality issues.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion tells lenders and the council's own finance director that the financial statements cannot be relied upon. This creates uncertainty about the council's actual financial position and raises governance concerns.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinion issued 31 March 2025; auditors assessing progress against multi-year rebuild timescale (2023/24 onwards)
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a disclaimer audit opinion was issued, which drew attention to the potential issue on the quality of audit evidence for the valuation of PPE and investment property valued at EUV and FV

findings.headline: Material weaknesses in governance, control and oversight identified across multiple service areas with no or limited assurance audit opinions
findings.detail: Audits across four service areas received limited assurance (Clean Streets, Building Control, Cyber Security, HR agency staff), with weaknesses in outdated policies, incomplete record-keeping, and insufficient monitoring compounding control failures.
findings.matters: Multiple control weaknesses across different services suggest systemic governance issues affecting financial controls, service delivery capability, and ability to manage risk effectively.
findings.figures: 4 limited assurance audits; 1 no assurance audit; 5 service areas with identified governance weaknesses
findings.quote: Review and update of policies, processes and procedures – material weaknesses in governance, control and oversight were identified during several internal audit reviews completed across the year resulting in either no or limited assurance.

findings.headline: Housing Asset Management audit concluded with no assurance, the lowest audit opinion, on repairs and maintenance of council housing stock
findings.detail: One internal audit on Housing Asset Management – Repairs and Maintenance received no assurance opinion, indicating pervasive control weaknesses. An action plan is in place with a new repairs contract starting August 2026.
findings.matters: No assurance on asset repairs and maintenance suggests serious gaps in controls over council housing stock upkeep, affecting asset condition and potentially requiring unplanned expenditure.
findings.figures: 1 no assurance audit; repairs contract implementation target August 2026
findings.quote: There was one internal audit review that concluded with no assurance and refers to the following: o Housing Asset Management – Repairs and Maintenance

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued judgment of serious failings in council's housing safety and accountability standards
findings.detail: Following self-referral to the regulator, a formal judgment found serious failings in how the council delivers consumer standards relating to Safety and Quality (gas, electrical, asbestos, fire, water, lift safety) and Transparency, Influence and Accountability. An action plan is in place with adoption of new policies and procedures.
findings.matters: A regulator's judgment of serious failings in landlord safety standards signals control weaknesses in a major council asset class and regulatory risk that could affect service delivery and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Six safety compliance areas identified: gas, electrical, asbestos, fire, water, and lift safety
findings.quote: Following self-referral to the Regulator of Social Housing a Regulator Judgement was issued that found serious failings in how the council is delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards in relation to the Safety and Quality Standard and the Transparency, Influence and Accountability Standard.

findings.headline: Council took £10m of new PWLB borrowing in the year, increasing total debt to £159.3m
findings.detail: Winchester borrowed £10m in two tranches (December and March) from the Public Works Loan Board via Equal Instalments of Principal loans, while repaying £5.2m at maturity. Net borrowing increased by £4.8m in the year. Total outstanding debt is now £159.3m at a weighted average rate of 3.06% with 17.8 years average maturity. All borrowing relates to the Housing Revenue Account.
findings.matters: A lender tracking Winchester's debt trajectory needs to see the actual borrowing executed and understand the terms. HRA dominance (£212.5m of £280.8m total CFR) is material and typical for councils with significant housing stock.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £159.3m; new PWLB borrowing £10m; repayments £5.2m; weighted average rate 3.06%; weighted average maturity 17.8 years; HRA CFR £212.5m of total CFR £280.8m
findings.quote: Net borrowing increased by 4.8m in the year. This consisted of £10m of new PWLB borrowing taken in two £5m tranches in December and March, both of which were Equal Instalments of Principal (EIP) loans, offset by the repayment of £5m at maturity and £0.2m of EIP loans – all from the PWLB.

findings.headline: Investment income substantially exceeded budget due to higher interest rates and larger cash balances
findings.detail: Winchester achieved £1.4m of investment income against a budget of £0.6m, delivering an additional £0.8m above budget. This outperformance was driven by interest rates remaining higher for longer than expected and the council holding higher average investment balances (£34.2m average portfolio yielding 4.1%) than forecast.
findings.matters: Investment income is discretionary and volatile, dependent on interest rates and cash position. While positive in the short term, a lender would note this benefit may not continue if interest rates fall as forecast.
findings.figures: Investment income outturn £1.4m vs budget £0.6m; average investment portfolio £34.2m at 4.1% yield; prior year £1.64m on £34.1m portfolio at 4.81%
findings.quote: The 2025/26 outturn shows £1.4m of income achieved against a budget of £0.6m, delivering an additional £0.8m of income above budget. This was a consequence of interest rates continuing to remain higher for longer than anticipated and higher average balances than forecast during the year.

findings.headline: Council forecasts significant additional borrowing requirement from 2026/27 to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The liability benchmark (lowest risk borrowing level) shows Winchester will need to borrow substantially more money in coming years. By 2028, the benchmark is forecast to be £201.1m while existing borrowing is only £136.8m, creating a gap of £64.3m that must be filled through new borrowing. The council's capital financing requirement is forecast to rise to £301.2m by 2028, driving this increased need.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's forward borrowing trajectory and whether it is manageable. This shows Winchester's debt will increase meaningfully if it proceeds with its planned capital programme.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark 2028: £201.1m; existing borrowing forecast 2028: £136.8m; CFR forecast 2028: £301.2m; balance sheet resources forecast to decline from £136.1m (2026) to £110.1m (2028)
findings.quote: Table 7 and Graph 1 illustrate the council expects a positive liability benchmark across the forecast period, which generally means an authority is required to take external borrowing to fund the gap between its resources and the CFR.

findings.headline: Reserves must be held to maintain assets through local government reorganisation in April 2028
findings.detail: The council notes explicitly that reserves must be sufficient to maintain and refurbish its existing estate up to and beyond Local Government Reorganisation, when a unitary authority will take control. This is the first time in the planning period that control shifts, creating transition risk.
findings.matters: Under-provisioned reserves could force unplanned borrowing or defer maintenance post-transition, affecting service quality and asset condition. Lenders monitor reserve adequacy through planned transitions.
findings.figures: LGR transition date: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The council needs to ensure that sufficient reserves are in place to maintain and refurbish its existing estate up to and beyond Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: 1000-home housing programme relies on ambitious capital spending amid rising costs
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme includes £181m over ten years for new build to deliver 1000 homes, alongside £96.2m for major repairs including fire safety, roof replacements, windows and doors, electrical and heating systems, and kitchens. Individual schemes are assessed annually for affordability within the 30-year HRA Business Plan.
findings.matters: An ambitious housing build programme at a time of rising costs and rates means delivery risk is elevated; for a lender, this tracks whether the council's housing ambitions remain achievable without requiring unplanned revenue support.
findings.figures: £181.0m budgeted for new build over 10 years; £96.2m for major repairs; total HRA capital £329.5m
findings.quote: An estimated £96.2m £96.2m will be spent on major repairs and maintenance of our existing housing stock including £10.3m to improve fire safety; £6.8m on roof replacements for dwellings; £13.3m on windows & doors for dwellings; £2.2m for estate improvements; £18.6m for major works to blocks

findings.headline: Rising interest rates and construction inflation now challenge the viability of planned build projects
findings.detail: Borrowing costs have trebled in three years (from ~2% in late 2021 to 5-6% in late 2025). Combined with significant construction inflation, the council now faces explicit constraints on which housing and regeneration projects can proceed.
findings.matters: Cost inflation eroding project returns signals the council may not deliver the planned capital programme, affecting regeneration and housing goals; rising rates also directly increase MRP and financing cost burden.
findings.figures: Interest rates: circa 2% (end 2021) to between 5% and 6% (end 2025)
findings.quote: The cost of borrowing has increased considerably in the last few years (rates available to the council at the end of 2021 were circa 2% and at the end of 2025 were between 5% and 6%). This, coupled with significant construction inflation, challenges the viability of potential build projects.

findings.headline: Guildhall condition survey identified £3.3m unplanned capital works
findings.detail: A recent condition survey found up to £5m of works needed to the listed Guildhall, of which £3.3m is classified as capital expenditure. These works address fire safety and utility improvements to enhance letting potential. The works are now included in the approved capital programme.
findings.matters: Unplanned capital maintenance on significant council assets can crowd out planned investment and force additional borrowing; the inclusion signals the council's estate condition risk is being actively managed.
findings.figures: £5m total works needed; £3.3m capital element
findings.quote: A recent condition survey has indicated that works of up to £5m are required to the Guildhall of which an estimated £3.3m are capital.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs forecast to rise from 13.9% of net revenue stream in 2024/25 to 17.0% by 2028/29
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account financing costs (interest and MRP on debt) are forecast to rise from 13.9% of net revenue stream in 2024/25 to 17.0% by 2028/29. HRA financing costs themselves will rise from £5.2m to £7.7m over the period. This directly reduces the HRA's capacity to fund repairs, maintenance, or tenant services without rent increases.
findings.matters: A rising proportion of rental income consumed by financing costs indicates the housing business plan is becoming more constrained; lenders track this ratio as a key stress indicator for council landlords.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: £5.2m (2024/25 actual) to £7.7m (2028/29 budget); HRA proportion of net revenue stream: 13.9% to 17.0%
findings.quote: HRA proportion of net revenue stream 13.9% 13.5% 13.3% 15.8% 17.0%

findings.headline: Significant increase in external borrowing as internal resources deplete
findings.detail: The council has had sufficient cash and investment balances to internally borrow much of its capital financing requirement, but now needs to increase external borrowing for the first time. HRA borrowing alone is forecast to grow from £212.5m to £247.3m by 2028/29. The council is using treasury advisors (Arlingclose) to optimise borrowing strategy.
findings.matters: A material shift from internal to external borrowing signals depleting reserves and increased debt service risk, a key concern for lenders on the council's financial capacity.
findings.figures: HRA CFR: £212.5m (31.3.2025) to £247.3m (31.3.2029); Total borrowing in capital financing: £150.7m over 10 years
findings.quote: The council has had sufficient cash and investment balances to be able to internally borrow a significant element of its CFR but will, need to increase its external borrowing in addition to the £159.4m (as at 31 December 2025) of borrowing the council has currently externalised on behalf of the HRA.

findings.headline: The IFRS 9 statutory override exempting the council from recognizing pooled fund gains and losses in its accounts expires on 31 March 2028, exposing future financial statements to property market volatility.
findings.detail: Winchester holds £5m in a pooled property fund, currently valued with an unrealised gain of £0.2777m. The statutory override that exempts local authorities from recognizing such gains and losses in their accounts expires on 31 March 2028. From that date onwards, any falls in the fund's market value will create accounting losses that directly impact the council's reported reserves and financial position.
findings.matters: A significant property market downturn after 2028 could create unexpected accounting write-downs, damaging reported reserves and potentially affecting the council's perceived creditworthiness. The council needs to consider whether to hold, hedge, or redeem this investment before the 2028 deadline.
findings.figures: £5m pooled property fund; £0.2777m current unrealised capital gain; exemption expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: This override has been extended to 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024, at which time the council will be expected to reflect any gains and losses in the CIES.

findings.headline: The council will require up to £66.5m in additional external borrowing by 2029 to fund its capital programme as reserves are depleted.
findings.detail: The council's capital financing requirement is forecast to rise from £281.9m to £316.5m by 2029. Currently using internal borrowing (drawing down reserves) to minimize external debt, the council's balance sheet resources are forecast to decline from £141.4m to £104.5m over four years. This will force the council to take external borrowing to continue funding its capital programme, with a maximum of £66.5m potentially required to maintain minimum liquidity reserves while delivering the planned capital spend.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand planned borrowing volumes, timing, and the resulting increase in debt service costs. This materially affects the council's debt trajectory and revenue budget sustainability over the medium term.
findings.figures: Maximum £66.5m additional external borrowing required; CFR rising from £281.9m (31/03/26) to £316.5m (31/03/29); reserves declining from £141.4m to £104.5m; liability benchmark rising from £159.7m to £221.0m over the same period
findings.quote: It is anticipated that to keep debt at a minimum level, a maximum of £66.5m of additional debt would need to be taken out.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation to unitary authority on 1 April 2028 creates decision-making uncertainty and unfunded transition costs
findings.detail: Winchester will merge into a unitary authority in April 2028. The business plan includes 'forecast capital expenditure beyond that date only includes projects to which the council will be contractually committed' and notes that 'decisions relating to the HRA after April 2028, unless contractually committed, will be the decisions of the new unitary authority.' The HRA operating account (Appendix 6) only forecasts to 2054/55, but the timing and terms of the transition are uncertain. Paragraph 11.5 of the risk section notes that 'decision making beyond September 2026 may be delayed if authorisations are required from Secretary of State and/or the new organisation.'
findings.matters: Organisational upheaval creates implementation risk for capital projects, potential delays in decision-making, and uncertainty about staffing and system integration costs. The business plan's assumptions beyond April 2028 may not hold if the new authority has different priorities or fiscal constraints.
findings.figures: Merger date: 1 April 2028; potential decision-making delays from September 2026 onward; HRA business plan extends 30 years but assumes significant transition uncertainty after 2028
findings.quote: The timetable for local government reorganisation means that the council is expected to become part of a unitary council from 1 April 2028... decisions relating to the HRA after April 2028, unless contractually committed, will be the decisions of the new unitary authority

findings.headline: Government withdrawal of Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund grant for battery installations forced mid-programme replanning and relinquishment of £3.5m-equivalent funding
findings.detail: In December 2025, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) withheld funding for battery installations, requiring the retrofit team to replan. Winchester has decided to 'relinquish the funding from DESNZ' and change delivery strategy mid-stream, moving away from the complex PAS 2035 framework to simpler single-measure delivery. While the council estimates £0.95m saving from this approach, the change demonstrates vulnerability to central government funding decisions and adds execution risk to the £41.8m retrofit capital programme needed to meet EPC-C requirements by 2030/31.
findings.matters: The HRA is dependent on government grant funding for its decarbonisation targets and financial plan. Withdrawal or policy changes mid-programme force costly replanning and create uncertainty about whether EPC-C targets (a regulatory requirement) can be met on current budgets.
findings.figures: SHF funding relinquished; estimated cost savings from replanning £0.95m; retrofit capital programme £41.8m remaining within budget; regulatory requirement EPC-C by 2030/31
findings.quote: It has been proposed by the Retrofit team that Winchester City Council relinquish the funding from DESNZ due to the loss in revenue caused by the hold on battery installations... this allows the Retrofit team to focus on the easier to treat homes and move to a single measure delivery on the harder to treat properties

findings.headline: PWLB borrowing costs remain elevated above 5% despite base rate reductions; £85m of existing debt requires refinancing by 2042, with £35m in next 5 years at higher rates
findings.detail: The document states PWLB rates 'continue to remain higher than the period of historically low rates since 2008' and 'have remained well above 5% since the Summer.' Current external debt of £154.5m is fixed at average 3.2%, but £85m of this debt comes due for refinancing between now and 2042, of which £35m falls within 5 years. New borrowing assumptions are set at 5.75%, and refinancing maturing debt at higher rates increases annual interest costs. Interest costs have risen by £0.85m in the 2026/27 budget despite no new borrowing being anticipated.
findings.matters: The HRA faces a significant refinancing wall starting in the near term. Higher refinance costs will squeeze the operating budget and reduce capacity to invest in stock maintenance or new builds, or will require further rent increases to tenants.
findings.figures: £85m of existing debt due for refinancing by 2042; £35m within 5 years; current cost of external debt £5.2m/annum; new borrowing rate 5.75%; interest budget increase £0.85m in 2026/27; cost of external debt at average 3.2%
findings.quote: PWLB rates are not directly linked to the Bank of England base rate but are set at a margin over government gilt yields, which continue to remain higher than the period of historically low rates since 2008... the cost of borrowing remains elevated when compared to the previous ten years and remains a key risk to the HRA

findings.headline: Rent convergence savings postponed due to government delay, requiring additional £0.35m of emergency savings identified in February 2026
findings.detail: Government announcement on rent convergence (allowing additional increases of £1-£2 per week above CPI+1%) was postponed from November 2025 budget to January 2026, too late for 2026/27 implementation. This forced removal of expected savings and the identification of additional revenue savings including a 2% vacancy management target and reductions in staffing and supply budgets (Appendix 7). The document states 'it is critical that these savings are achieved, as failure to do so will reduce borrowing headroom and would result in significant cuts to the capital programme.'
findings.matters: The HRA's financial plan is dependent on achieving savings that are contingent on government policy announcements and staffing efficiency targets. Failure to deliver creates pressure to cut the capital programme or increase borrowing, both of which increase risk.
findings.figures: Original savings target £1m; additional savings required £0.45m (assumption changes) + £0.35m (additional budget cuts) = total £1.13m
findings.quote: It is critical that these savings are achieved, as failure to do so will reduce borrowing headroom and would result in significant cuts to the capital programme.

findings.headline: New build programme is not financially self-supporting; new homes require ongoing subsidy from Right to Buy receipts, s106 contributions, or government grants
findings.detail: The council's evaluation shows that 'it is no longer possible without heavy subsidy from Right to Buy receipts, s106 affordable housing contributions or government grants' to construct or acquire properties financed through rents. Once these funding streams are exhausted, 'it will fall to wider rent payers to subsidise new build.' The 1000 homes programme depends on prudential borrowing of £141.4m (39% of total capital funding), making its affordability contingent on rent growth and grant availability.
findings.matters: A lender to Winchester needs to understand that the HRA's expansion of stock requires cross-subsidy from existing tenants and external grants, not rental revenue alone. This increases financial fragility if grants cease or rent-setting policy tightens.
findings.figures: New build capital requirement £202.8m over 10 years; prudential borrowing £141.4m (39% of funding); construction cost £450,000-£500,000 per property (90sqm 3-bed)
findings.quote: it is no longer possible without heavy subsidy from Right to Buy receipts, s106 affordable housing contributions or government grants, and ultimately, once these funding streams are exhausted, it will fall to wider rent payers to subsidise new build

findings.headline: HRA working balance projected to decline from £13.6m in 2025/26 to £8.2m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The operating account shows opening balance of £13.6m in 2025/26 falling to £10.1m in 2026/27 (Appendix 1), and further to £8.2m by year 3 (Appendix 6). While described as part of the long-term plan, the rate of decline limits headroom for unexpected costs or policy changes, particularly concerning given local government reorganisation in April 2028.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the HRA's financial resilience and borrowing headroom at a time when it is taking on significant new debt for the 1000 homes programme.
findings.quote: Projected Balance at Year End 13,648,672... 10,119,878

findings.headline: Non-Domestic Rate (NNDR) and other debt write-offs signal collection difficulties: £228k NNDR plus £53k tenant arrears approved for write-off
findings.detail: Cabinet approval is sought to write off three NNDR debts totalling £228,435.25 'as there are no longer options available to the council to recover any payment. The debts have all gone through an insolvency process.' Additionally, £53,649.94 is approved for write-off against Provident Asset Management (rent arrears £27,649.94 plus dilapidation £26,000). While the paper notes this is a 'last resort' approach, the accumulated write-offs signal collection difficulties in both business rates and property income.
findings.matters: Accumulated write-offs (£281k+) indicate income collection risk and suggest the council's revenue forecasts may not fully reflect collection slippage or insolvency risk in its debtors.
findings.figures: £228,435.25 NNDR write-offs (three debts); £27,649.94 rent arrears write-off (Provident Asset Management); £26,000 dilapidation liability write-off; total £281,085.19
findings.quote: There are three debts included at Appendix F, for uncollected Non-Domestic Rates. Cabinet approval for the write-off of these debts is sought in accordance with Financial Procedure Rule 12.7(f), as there are no longer options available to the council to recover any payment. The debts have all gone through an insolvency process, of one variation or another.

findings.headline: Utility costs rising: £150k budget increase approved for 2026/27, with additional adverse variance of £150k forecast in 2025/26
findings.detail: The budget includes a growth allocation of £150k for utilities in 2026/27 'in order to cover the additional forecast utility costs from 2026/27.' Additionally, the 2025/26 forecast outturn reports £150k as an adverse service variance for 'Increased Utility costs.' This indicates ongoing and unabating cost pressures beyond the inflation assumption in the budget.
findings.matters: Persistent and growing utility cost pressures suggest either underlying energy price inflation is outpacing the council's forecasts, or consumption is rising. Either way, this is a leading indicator of ongoing revenue pressure.
findings.figures: £150k growth for utilities 2026/27; £150k adverse variance in 2025/26 for increased utility costs
findings.quote: Increased Utility costs - £150,000 [2025/26 adverse variance]. Utility budget increased by £150,000 in order to cover the additional forecast utility costs from 2026/27.

findings.headline: Investment property portfolio of £69m (of £176.2m total) held for rental income; risk register identifies tenant failure risk
findings.detail: The council holds £69m in investment properties within a £176.2m property portfolio. The risk register explicitly identifies 'Commercial tenants unable to pay rents or subject to business failure' as a material risk, noting 'Close monitoring of rent position by property team with support to tenants through effective working relationships.' The budget also records £60k adverse variance in 2025/26 'Reduced Guildhall Income' and the paper approves write-off of Provident Asset Management rent arrears (£27,649.94) and dilapidation liabilities (£26,000).
findings.matters: A £69m investment property income stream is material to the council's overall financial stability. Tenant difficulties (explicitly identified as a risk) or broader commercial property slowdown could materially impact income and worsen the forecast deficit.
findings.figures: £69m in investment properties; £176.2m total property portfolio; 2025/26 Guildhall income adverse variance £60k; Provident Asset Management write-off £53,649.94
findings.quote: The council's General Fund has a property portfolio valued at £176.2m as at 31 March 2025 of which £69m is classified as investment properties (held solely for rental income and/or capital appreciation). [Risk register] Commercial tenants unable to pay rents or subject to business failure.

findings.headline: Major Investment Reserve reduced to £4.3m uncommitted with £3m reallocated to property maintenance
findings.detail: The council transfers £2m from Major Investment Reserve to Property Reserve and £1m to Car Parks Property Reserve (£3m total) to fund maintenance rather than new investment. The paper states 'only just over £4.3m remaining in that reserve and all future business cases for regeneration work will need to take this into account (a clearer and stronger focus on financial viability).' This implies future capital projects are now heavily scrutinised and constrained.
findings.matters: Exhaustion of discretionary capital reserves means the council has lost flexibility to respond to emerging capital needs, invest in regeneration, or support economic development. All future capital expenditure competes against a thin reserve base.
findings.figures: £4.3m remaining in Major Investment Reserve; £2m transferred to Property Reserve; £1m transferred to Car Parks Reserve; only ~£1.3m uncommitted after these transfers
findings.quote: With existing commitments, there is only just over £4.3m remaining in that reserve and all future business cases for regeneration work will need to take this into account (a clearer and stronger focus on financial viability). Whilst many costs can be capitalised and funded from borrowing if works proceed, upfront investment has been high for previous projects, arguably with insufficient focus on cost recovery.

findings.headline: Guildhall requires £1.7m emergency revenue spend for essential structural and roof repairs, part of £5m condition survey findings
findings.detail: The budget approves £1.7m for 'essential structural and repair works to the Guildhall to maintain this listed civic building.' This is described as 'required prior to further decision making on the future operating model of the Guildhall and Abbey House' and is part of a £5m package identified in a recent condition survey. Breakdown includes £600k roof repairs, £300k stonework, £300k windows, £200k internal decoration, £100k external decoration, £100k professional fees, £100k carpets. Scrutiny also raised concern about 'deteriorating condition of the former River Park Leisure Centre site.'
findings.matters: Material deferred maintenance on civic assets signals either prior underfunding of asset management or deteriorating asset condition (or both). A listed building with structural issues creates both financial and reputational risk.
findings.figures: £1.7m revenue; £5m total package; breakdown: roof £600k, stonework £300k, windows £300k, internal £200k, external £100k, fees £100k, carpets £100k
findings.quote: A revenue budget of £1.7m has been included for essential works to the Guildhall. This is part of a package of capital and revenue works totalling £5m and identified in a recent condition survey.

findings.headline: Transformation Challenge 2025 is delivering only half of its £3m annual savings target, per scrutiny concerns
findings.detail: Scrutiny Committee raised concern that 'TC25 delivering only half of its £3m annual savings target.' The budget notes only £56k of net additional savings in this report and total TC25 savings to date of £1.675m. This suggests the £3m annual target is not being consistently hit and the transformation programme—central to the council's medium-term strategy—is underperforming.
findings.matters: If the primary cost-control programme is only delivering 50% of target, the council's financial strategy is weaker than planned and there is hidden scope for further deficits or the need for additional unplanned savings.
findings.figures: £3m annual savings target; £1.675m total TC25 savings to date; £56k additional savings in this budget; scrutiny notes only 50% of target being achieved
findings.quote: Scrutiny Committee is due to consider this report at its meeting on 10 February 2026, after this report has been dispatched. Any matters that the Scrutiny Committee wishes to raise or asks the Cabinet to note before making their decision will be reported and considered fully at the Cabinet meeting. [Earlier context] questions about TC25 delivering only half of its £3m annual savings target

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation implementation costs are unknown but forecast to consume the Transitional Reserve (£8m), leaving zero for further transformation investment
findings.detail: The paper states 'The implementation cost to Winchester of Local Government Reorganisation cannot be known until the Government decides the final configuration in March 2026.' Hampshire/Isle of Wight LGR submissions cited costs between £128m-£132m across the region. The council has designated the Transitional Reserve (£8m uncommitted balance) as 'the first funding source for the council's contribution towards these implementation costs' and notes 'this reserve will... almost certainly... [be] multiple millions of pounds, leaving none for further investment by the existing council.' This is a material contingent liability with timing uncertainty.
findings.matters: If LGR costs consume £8m+ of the Transitional Reserve, the council loses its transformation funding buffer precisely when it needs to manage a transition. This forces a choice between LGR readiness and baseline service delivery.
findings.figures: £128m-£132m regional cost estimate; £8m uncommitted Transitional Reserve balance; forecast contribution described as 'almost certain... multiple millions'
findings.quote: The implementation cost to Winchester of Local Government Reorganisation cannot be known until the Government decides the final configuration in March 2026. The LGR submissions highlighted costs to the entire Hampshire & Isle of Wight area of between £128m and £132m.

findings.headline: Forecast deficits of £3.6m in 2029/30 rising to £7.2m by 2034/35, driven by government's business rates reset
findings.detail: The council explicitly forecasts 'a significant deficit of £3.6m is forecast for 2029/30, increasing to £7.2m by 2034/35.' The root cause is the 'full baseline reset of business rates' from Fair Funding 2.0: Winchester's ten years of strong business growth gave it retained a higher proportion of business rates locally; the reset redistributes much of that growth nationally. This creates a structural funding gap the council cannot control or solve within its existing strategy.
findings.matters: A structural funding cliff in 2029 onwards means the council will either have to significantly reduce services, materially increase borrowing, or both. Lenders need to know whether the council has credible plans to address this beyond hoping for unitary reorganisation.
findings.quote: A significant deficit of £3.6m is forecast for 2029/30, increasing to £7.2m by 2034/35. However, it should be noted that not only are forecasts after 2028/29 subject to a high degree of uncertainty, but they also relate to the period beyond LGR, and therefore to the planning window for the new unitary council.

findings.headline: Disrepair claims are emerging as an increasing liability with new claims continuing to arrive
findings.detail: The council is settling historic disrepair claims and continues to receive new claims, attributed to 'increased awareness of ability to claim'. A provision was established with £0.17m charged to 2024/25 budget.
findings.matters: Emerging liability trends signal either mounting service delivery issues or cost drift from resident compensation; either way represents forward cost pressure on HRA
findings.figures: £0.17m provision charged in 2024/25; trend described as ongoing with new claims continuing
findings.quote: A number of historic disrepair claims are being settled, and the Council continues to receive new claims, in part due to increased awareness of ability to claim. A provision has been set up to provide for the settlement of these claims, which has led to an adverse variance of £0.17m.

findings.headline: Fire safety and asbestos compliance are creating new unbudgeted cost pressures of approximately £0.9m
findings.detail: Regulatory compliance inspections for fire safety and asbestos were not fully embedded in baseline budgets. The council identified potential revenue cost of £0.9m, with fire safety inspections well advanced and asbestos inspections commencing April 2025. These are new structural compliance costs.
findings.matters: Compliance costs are mandatory and non-discretionary; they represent new structural additions to baseline that cannot be deferred without regulatory risk
findings.figures: £0.9m potential revenue cost identified; inspections procured at £0.3m underspend against forecast
findings.quote: The quarterly forecast report identified a potential revenue cost of £0.9m for fire safety and asbestos compliance inspections and fire safety works.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing costs are rising due to higher PWLB interest rates, now at 5.45% vs 5% budgeted
findings.detail: The council holds £58.1m of internal borrowing (from reserves). The cost rose to 5.24% from 3.77% because 3-month PWLB rates averaged 5.45% against budget of 5%, creating £0.16m additional unbudgeted cost pressure in 2024/25.
findings.matters: The HRA has £212.6m underlying borrowing; higher financing costs reduce headroom and affordability if PWLB rates remain elevated or rise further
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £58.1m (up £5.2m); cost of capital 5.24% vs 3.77% prior year; 3-month PWLB 5.45% vs 5% budgeted; £0.16m cost overrun
findings.quote: However, internal borrowing costs were higher than forecast by £0.16m as the 3-month PWLB rate used to calculate the internal cost of borrowing averaged 5.45% across the year, compared to a budgeted rate of 5%.

findings.headline: Repairs costs are rising structurally with baseline inflation of £1.2m expected to continue
findings.detail: The HRA overspent repairs by £1.8m in 2024/25, comprising £1.2m baseline cost inflation from 2021-24 price rises, £0.4m from prior year under-accrual, and £0.1m fire safety compliance. This baseline increase is embedded in 2025/26 budgets and is ongoing structural.
findings.matters: Repairs are a core HRA operating cost; structural inflation here directly erodes financial capacity unless recovered through higher tenant rents or reduced service levels
findings.figures: £1.8m adverse variance in 2024/25; £1.2m baseline increase from inflation; repairs budget is core recurring cost
findings.quote: The overall adverse variance on repairs in 2024/25 was £1.8m, which includes an underestimate in 2023/24 cost accrual of £0.4m, and additional compliance costs for fire safety works of £0.1m in addition to the expected baseline increase of £1.2m.

findings.headline: Reserves grew by £10m to £49.5m, but significant unspent commitments are in place and the council is managing around funding uncertainty
findings.detail: General Fund earmarked reserves increased from £41.3m to £49.5m, with operational reserves now at £14.2m. However, the council explicitly states that significant commitments are in place against these balances and that it will continue to manage reserves prudently given uncertainty around funding and interest rates.
findings.matters: Reserves that are fully committed or earmarked for specific purposes cannot be relied upon for liquidity or to absorb unexpected shocks; the council's apparent reserve strength is less available than headline numbers suggest.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves increased from £41.3m to £49.5m; operational reserves £14.2m (up from £11.5m)
findings.quote: Careful management of earmarked reserves has resulted in a £10m increase in overall balances at the end of 2024/25. However, significant commitments are in place against these balances and along with continued uncertainty around funding and interest rates, the council will continue to manage reserves in a prudent manner.

findings.headline: Hampshire Community Bank investment of £188,000 was written off in full after the bank went into administration
findings.detail: In November 2024, Hampshire Community Bank went into administration. The council had purchased 188 shares totalling £188,000 and a planned purchase of an additional 62 shares for £62,000 was cancelled. All previously purchased shares were written out of the balance sheet as a loss.
findings.matters: Investment failures signal judgment issues and demonstrate the council is exposed to asset impairment risk; the council originally recognized this carried considerable risk when the investment was made.
findings.figures: Shares purchased £188,000 (written off); cancelled purchase £62,000
findings.quote: In November 2024, Hampshire Community Bank went into administration. The council had purchased 188 shares over three tranches totalling £188,000. As a consequence, the shares already purchased have been written out of the council's balance sheet and the fourth tranche purchase of an additional 62 shares at a cost of £62,000 will no longer go ahead.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 will materially change government funding from 2026/27, but remains unconfirmed
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that significant changes to funding are under review and expected to take effect in 2026/27. Until confirmed there remains significant uncertainty over medium-term funding levels. The council is attempting to model scenarios, but the outcome is not yet known.
findings.matters: A step-change in government funding could either relieve or sharply worsen the council's financial position; lenders cannot model cash flow with confidence until this is settled.
findings.figures: Changes expected 2026/27; timeframe currently unconfirmed
findings.quote: Significant changes to local council funding from central government are under review as part of the Government's Fair Funding Review 2.0 consultation exercise, with changes expected to take effect from 2026/27. These changes, which have long been expected, will hopefully bring a multi-year settlement to give greater certainty over the medium-term once confirmed. However, until confirmed there remains significant uncertainty over medium-term funding levels.

findings.headline: The £2.4m favorable outturn was heavily dependent on £1.1m of additional interest receivable from higher rates and higher than expected balances
findings.detail: More than 45% of the favorable variance came from higher interest income, driven by higher cash balances (particularly s106 balances) and higher interest rates. If interest rates fall or if the council is forced to deploy cash for spending, this income advantage disappears immediately.
findings.matters: Favorable variances built on interest rate support are not sustainable and do not reflect operational tightness; when rates normalize the council reverts to underlying budget pressures.
findings.figures: Additional interest receivable £1.1m; total favorable variance £2.4m
findings.quote: Additional net interest receivable of £1.1m caused by higher than expected balances (specifically s106 balances) and higher than forecast rates of return.

findings.headline: Business rates collection deteriorated, with a £1.1m adverse variance from doubtful debts and appeals
findings.detail: The council collects over £60m in business rates annually, but 2024/25 saw a £1.1m deficit compared to budget. This was driven by increasing the allowance for doubtful debts and a significant increase in the appeals provision, suggesting either economic weakness in the district or structural collection challenges.
findings.matters: Business rates form a significant part of local council income; deterioration signals either that local businesses are struggling or that the council faces a harder collection environment, both of which affect repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Total collectable business rates over £60m; adverse variance £1.1m
findings.quote: Business Rates – The total collectable business rates for 2024/25 were over £60m within the year including significant ongoing and new reliefs. The outturn deficit of £1.1m related mainly to increasing the allowance for doubtful debts and a significant increase in the appeals provision.
